title: 1 Chronicles 5:1–10
context: The Chronicler turns to the tribes east of the Jordan, beginning with Reuben. Verses 1–2 explain why Reuben, though firstborn, does not head the genealogies: because he defiled his father’s couch (compare Genesis 35:22; 49:3–4), the birthright went to the sons of Joseph, whom Jacob had adopted and blessed (compare Genesis 48), while Judah prevailed and from him came the prince. The Chronicler thus distinguishes the birthright from leadership and explains the order of his lists without denying Reuben’s place. The Reubenite line is traced to Beerah, whom Tilgath Pilneser king of Assyria carried away captive (5:6; compare 2 Kings 15:29), and the tribe’s territory and a war with the Hagrites in the days of Saul are noted (5:8–10). The Reuben lists can be compared with Genesis 46:9 and Numbers 26:5–11 without harmonizing differences. The identity of the Hagrites and the exact extent of the territory are uncertain. Both traditions read the section as shared ground about the lasting consequences of sin, God’s sovereign ordering of Israel’s leadership, and his continued care for a tribe that lost its preeminence.

verses.text: The sons of Reuben the firstborn of Israel (for he was the firstborn, but because he defiled his father’s couch, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph the son of Israel; and the genealogy is not to be listed according to the birthright.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Reuben’s loss of the birthright is tied directly to his own act of defiling his father’s couch (compare Genesis 35:22; 49:3–4). The verse shows that sin has real consequences that can reach across generations, while the Chronicler still lists Reuben’s sons and keeps the tribe within Israel’s genealogy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the transfer of the birthright to Joseph’s sons as both a consequence of Reuben’s sin and an outworking of God’s ordering of Jacob’s family, recalling Jacob’s blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh in Genesis 48. Both traditions agree that the verse joins human responsibility and divine purpose, and that the Chronicler explains the order of his lists rather than erasing Reuben.

verses.text: For Judah prevailed above his brothers, and from him came the prince; but the birthright was Joseph’s)—
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that the Chronicler distinguishes two honors: Judah prevailed and from him came the prince, while the birthright was Joseph’s. The verse prepares for the central place of David’s house in the book and shows that God’s purposes for leadership did not depend on birth order alone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see in Judah’s rise the outworking of God’s purpose announced in Jacob’s blessing (compare Genesis 49:8–10), which the Chronicler connects with the royal line. Both traditions agree that the verse affirms both Joseph’s birthright and Judah’s leadership without setting them against each other, and that God freely orders his people’s history.

verses.text: the sons of Reuben the firstborn of Israel: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that after the long explanation, the Chronicler returns to list the sons of Reuben: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi, the same four names found in Genesis 46:9 and Numbers 26:5–6. The tribe that lost its preeminence still receives its genealogy, a sign that God had not cast Reuben off.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the agreement with the earlier lists and see the verse as evidence of God’s faithfulness to Reuben’s descendants despite their forefather’s sin. Both traditions agree that loss of the birthright did not mean exclusion from the covenant people, and that the Chronicler includes Reuben fully among the tribes.

verses.text: The sons of Joel: Shemaiah his son, Gog his son, Shimei his son,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that the line of Joel is traced through Shemaiah, Gog, and Shimei, though the text does not say how Joel connects to the sons of Reuben in the previous verse. The Chronicler preserves the line as he received it, and the verse leads toward a prince of the Reubenites in a later generation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly leave the connection unstated where the text does not supply it. Both traditions agree that the chain of names carries the story of Reuben forward toward the Assyrian period, and that the Chronicler’s record keeps the memory of the tribe alive for readers who had themselves known exile.

verses.text: Micah his son, Reaiah his son, Baal his son,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the line continues through Micah, Reaiah, and Baal. The name Baal in an Israelite genealogy is recorded without comment, and readers should not draw conclusions about the person’s faith from the name alone; the verse continues the patient tracing of Reuben’s descendants.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise refrain from building on the name Baal, since the text gives no comment. Both traditions agree that the verse belongs to the Chronicler’s record of continuity within Reuben, a tribe whose long history in the land would end in captivity, as the next verse explains.

verses.text: and Beerah his son, whom Tilgath Pilneser king of Assyria carried away captive. He was prince of the Reubenites.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that Beerah, prince of the Reubenites, was carried away captive by Tilgath Pilneser king of Assyria. The verse connects the genealogy to the Assyrian deportations also described in 2 Kings 15:29, where the king’s name appears as Tiglath Pileser, and it introduces the theme of exile that will close the chapter.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the link to 2 Kings 15:29. Both traditions agree that the brief notice anticipates the explanation in 5:25–26, where the Chronicler presents the exile of the eastern tribes as the outcome of unfaithfulness under God’s hand.

verses.text: His brothers by their families, when the genealogy of their generations was listed: the chief, Jeiel, and Zechariah,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Beerah’s brothers are listed by their families when the genealogy was recorded, with Jeiel named as chief. The verse shows the tribe’s internal order and leadership, and the mention of a recorded genealogy reflects the importance of such records in Israel’s life before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the verse as evidence of the order and continuity the Chronicler values within each tribe. Both traditions agree that the leaders named here have no recorded deeds, yet their inclusion affirms that the families of Reuben were known and remembered as part of God’s people.

verses.text: and Bela the son of Azaz, the son of Shema, the son of Joel, who lived in Aroer, even to Nebo and Baal Meon;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that Bela, traced back to Joel, lived in Aroer and as far as Nebo and Baal Meon, towns east of the Jordan associated with Reuben’s territory. The verse anchors the genealogy in real places and shows the tribe settled in the land God had allotted beyond the river.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the geographic details and see them as part of the Chronicler’s interest in the tribes’ inheritance. Both traditions agree that the precise locations of some of these places are debated, and that the theological point lies in God’s gift of land to Reuben, recalling the allotment described in Numbers 32 and Joshua 13.

verses.text: and he lived eastward even to the entrance of the wilderness from the river Euphrates, because their livestock were multiplied in the land of Gilead.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Bela’s territory extended eastward toward the wilderness that reaches to the Euphrates, because their livestock had multiplied in Gilead. The verse gives a practical reason for the tribe’s expansion, rooted in the realities of pastoral life, without suggesting any special command.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly observe that the expansion is explained by the growth of the herds and see God’s provision in that increase, though the verse does not say so directly. Both traditions agree that the description of the territory should not be pressed for precise boundaries, and that the verse reflects God’s blessing on Reuben’s livelihood.

verses.text: In the days of Saul, they made war with the Hagrites, who fell by their hand; and they lived in their tents throughout all the land east of Gilead.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that in the days of Saul the Reubenites made war with the Hagrites, who fell by their hand, and that Reuben then lived in their tents east of Gilead. The identity of the Hagrites is uncertain. The verse anticipates the fuller account of war in 5:18–22, where the Chronicler explains the victory more fully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise leave the Hagrites’ identity open and see the verse as a brief preview of the later account. Both traditions agree that the Chronicler links the eastern tribes’ history to Saul’s reign and that the victory, here simply reported, will later be attributed to God’s help in response to the people’s trust.
